blurb: How AI hears and speaks: turning sound into words, making natural voices, real-time assistants, and the risk of cloned voices.

steps.p: A microphone measures air pressure thousands of times a second. Recorded speech is a long list of numbers — 16,000 per second is common for voice.

steps.h: Make a picture of the sound
steps.p: Those numbers are turned into a spectrogram: an image showing how strong each pitch (frequency) is at each moment. Each vowel and consonant has its own visible pattern.
steps.analogy: Like sheet music for any sound: time runs left to right, pitch goes bottom to top.

steps.p: An encoder processes the spectrogram like an image, and a decoder writes out the words, one token at a time — just like a chatbot writing text.
OpenAI's Whisper was trained on about 680,000 hours of audio from the web — many accents, languages and noisy rooms — which made it robust.
Accuracy is measured by word error rate: the share of words wrong, missing or wrongly added. Lower is better.

options: How strong each pitch is at each moment
How loud the room is in decibels only
cards.why: Pitch over time. Time runs across, frequency up the side, brightness shows strength. It turns hearing into a seeing problem.

cards.q: OpenAI trained Whisper on roughly how much transcribed audio?
cards.why: About 680,000 hours — roughly 77 years of nonstop listening. The variety mattered as much as the amount.

cards.statement: Most speech models read the raw sound numbers directly as their input.
cards.why: False. Most first convert audio into a spectrogram-like picture, which is easier to learn from than raw air-pressure readings.

cards.title: OpenAI released Whisper openly in September 2022.
cards.detail: It can also translate speech in many languages straight into English text. Being free to download made it a building block for countless transcription apps.

cards.statement: A speech recogniser's word error rate can be more than 100%.
cards.hint: Count the words it wrongly adds, too.
cards.why: True. Errors include inserted words. A system that invents lots of extra words can make more errors than there were words spoken.

steps.p: Old voices glued together tiny recorded snippets of a real person. Understandable, but choppy and robotic at the joins.
In 2016, DeepMind's WaveNet used a neural network to produce the sound wave directly, one tiny sample at a time. It sounded far more human.
steps.analogy: Instead of cutting up words from magazines, writing the letter by hand.

steps.p: To capture a pitch, you must measure the sound at least twice per wave. To capture up to 8,000 waves a second, you need 16,000 samples a second.
Neural codecs compress audio into short sequences of tokens. Then a language-model-style network can "write" speech the way it writes text.
Shown a few seconds of someone's voice, such models can continue in that voice. Useful for accessibility — and a gift to scammers.

cards.q: To capture pitches up to 8,000 waves per second, you must sample audio at least…
cards.why: 16,000 times. You need at least two measurements per wave to capture it. That's why 16,000 per second is standard for speech.

cards.q: Neural audio codecs convert audio into…
cards.why: Sound tokens. Once audio is tokens, the same next-token machinery that writes text can generate speech and music.

cards.statement: Modern voice cloning can imitate a voice from just a few seconds of audio.
cards.why: True. Research systems from 2023 onward needed only about 3–10 seconds. A short voicemail or video clip can be enough.

cards.title: WaveNet was so slow at first that one second of speech took far longer than a second to generate.
cards.detail: Producing tens of thousands of samples one by one was heavy work. Later techniques made it fast enough for Google to use WaveNet voices in its products.

cards.q: What made WaveNet's voices sound so much more natural than older systems?
options: It generated the sound wave directly with a neural network
cards.why: Generating, not stitching. Without joins between recorded snippets, the voice flowed naturally with realistic breaths and intonation.

cards.title: Talking to AI in real time

steps.p: In human conversation, the gap between one person stopping and the other starting is typically about 200 milliseconds — a fifth of a second.
Classic assistants pass the baton three times: speech → text, text → chatbot, chatbot's text → speech. Each hand-off adds delay.
Turning speech into plain text throws away tone, emotion, laughter and hesitation. The chatbot can't hear that you sounded upset.
steps.analogy: Reading a transcript of a phone call versus hearing it.

steps.h: One model, speech in and out
steps.p: Speech-to-speech models hear audio and answer in audio directly — faster and able to respond to how you said something.
Voice activity detection decides when you've started or stopped speaking. Get it wrong and the assistant interrupts you, or waits awkwardly.

cards.q: In human conversation, the typical gap between turns is about…
cards.why: About 200 ms. People start planning their reply before the other person finishes. Voice AI has to come close to feel natural.

cards.statement: Relay-style voice systems lose information like tone of voice.
cards.hint: What survives when speech becomes plain text?
cards.why: True. Plain text keeps the words but loses how they were said — sarcasm, worry, excitement.

options: When the user has started or stopped speaking
cards.why: Start and stop. It's surprisingly hard: a pause to think isn't the same as finishing your turn.

cards.title: Some voice models can listen and talk at the same time.
cards.detail: Called "full-duplex", they handle interruptions and small listener cues like "mm-hmm" while speaking, instead of strictly taking turns.

cards.q: The biggest speed gain from speech-to-speech models comes from…
options: Skipping the separate transcription and voice-generation stages
cards.hint: Look at the relay in step 2.
cards.why: Fewer hand-offs. One model doing the whole job removes the waiting between stages.

steps.p: Apps like Suno and Udio make full songs — vocals, instruments, lyrics — from a short text description.
Record labels argue these models learned from copyrighted songs without permission. In 2024 the major labels sued both companies.
A few seconds of someone's voice can be enough to fake them saying anything — used in scam calls pretending to be relatives in trouble.

items: Scammer grabs a voice clip online
Calls a relative: "I'm in trouble, send money"

steps.p: In 2024 a robocall faked President Biden's voice telling voters not to vote. Regulators then ruled AI voices in robocalls fall under existing bans.
Agree a private code word with family. A real emergency caller will know it; a cloned voice won't.
steps.analogy: Like a password, but for people you love.

cards.q: Who sued AI music companies Suno and Udio in 2024?
options: Major record labels, coordinated by the RIAA
cards.why: The major labels. They argued training on copyrighted recordings without a licence was infringement. The cases pushed the industry toward licensing deals.

cards.statement: Scammers have used cloned voices to impersonate family members asking for money.
cards.why: True. Police and consumer agencies have warned about it repeatedly. Urgency and a familiar voice are a powerful combination.

cards.title: In 2024, a robocall faked President Biden's voice to tell New Hampshire voters not to vote.
cards.detail: Soon after, the US Federal Communications Commission ruled that AI-generated voices in robocalls fall under existing restrictions on artificial voices.

cards.q: What's a simple, effective defence against voice-clone scams in a family?
options: Agree a private code word to confirm identity in emergencies
Change your phone number every month
cards.why: A code word. It's free and works however good the fake voice is. Hanging up and calling back on a known number also helps.

cards.title: Set a family code word
cards.body: Pick a word only your close family knows. If anyone calls in a panic asking for money, ask for it.
cards.challenge: Message one family member today and agree on a code word for emergencies.
